DISPLACED JANITOR OPPORTUNITY ACT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Building Services, Inc.

DISPLACED JANITOR OPPORTUNITY ACT — TRANSITION RECORD
DISPLACED JANITOR OPPORTUNITY ACT — TRANSITION RECORD

Company completing this record: Acme Building Services, Inc.
Site(s)/facility covered by the service contract: 123 Main St office building, floors 1-10
Effective date of the successor service contract (or of the change to in-house building maintenance): November 1, 2026

Statement regarding retention of the predecessor contractor's or subcontractor's employees at the site(s) identified above: All 12 eligible employees were offered retention in writing on October 15, 2026

Statement regarding any employees not offered retention for cause: None; alternatively, describe the employee(s) and the stated cause

This record documents, as of the date signed below, Acme Building Services, Inc.'s actions with respect to the transition described above under California's Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, Labor Code §§ 1060-1065.

WHO AND WHAT THE ACT COVERS
California's Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act applies only within a specific set of defined terms. A "contractor" for purposes of the chapter is limited to a person that employs 25 or more individuals and that enters into a service contract with an "awarding authority" (the person awarding janitorial or building-maintenance service contracts, including subcontracts). Not every worker at a covered site is a covered "employee": the definition is limited to a service employee who works at least 15 hours per week, whose primary place of employment is in California, working under a contract to provide janitorial or building-maintenance services — and it expressly excludes managerial, supervisory, or confidential employees, including anyone who would be classified that way under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act. The obligations described in the clauses below apply only when a "successor service contract" exists: a service contract to perform essentially the same services previously performed under a different service contract at the same facility that terminated within the previous 30 days. A contract entered into more than 30 days after the predecessor contract terminated is still treated as a "successor service contract" if its execution was delayed for the purpose of avoiding the chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "“Contractor” means any person that employs 25 or more individuals and that enters into a service contract with the awarding authority."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1060(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, "contractor" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1060.)
  "“Employee” means any person employed as a service employee of a contractor or subcontractor who works at least 15 hours per week and whose primary place of employment is in the State of California under a contract to provide janitorial or building maintenance services. “Employee” does not include a person who is a managerial, supervisory, or confidential employee, including those employees who would be so defined under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1060(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, "employee" definition and exclusions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1060.)
  "“Successor service contract” means a service contract for the performance of essentially the same services as were previously performed pursuant to a different service contract at the same facility that terminated within the previous 30 days. A service contract entered into more than 30 days after the termination of a predecessor service contract shall be considered a “successor service contract” if its execution was delayed for the purpose of avoiding application of this chapter."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1060(g) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, "successor service contract" definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1060.)
  Known gap: All three quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1060) rather than independently authored sources. This clause does not address the separate defined terms in § 1060 for "person," "service contract," or "subcontractor," which are more mechanical in nature and are used, where relevant, in the other clauses of this document.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A COVERED CONTRACT IS TERMINATED
The chain of obligations under the Act begins when an awarding authority notifies a contractor that a covered service contract has been or will be terminated. At that point the awarding authority must state, in that same notification, whether a successor service contract has been or will be awarded, and if so, must identify the successor contractor by name and address. The terminated contractor then has a short, fixed window — three working days after receiving that notification — to provide the identified successor contractor with the name, date of hire, and job classification of each employee working at the site(s) covered by the terminated contract at the time of termination. If the terminated contractor does not yet know who the successor contractor is, that same employee information instead goes to the awarding authority, which becomes responsible for passing it along once a successor has been selected. These notice and information-transfer duties apply equally to subcontractors of a terminated contractor, not just to the prime contractor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "If an awarding authority notifies a contractor that the service contract between the awarding authority and the contractor has been terminated or will be terminated, the awarding authority shall indicate in that notification whether a successor service contract has been or will be awarded in its place and, if so, shall identify the name and address of the successor contractor. The terminated contractor shall, within three working days after receiving that notification, provide to the successor contractor identified by the awarding authority, the name, date of hire, and job classification of each employee employed at the site or sites covered by the terminated service contract at the time of the contract termination."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(a)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, termination notice and employee-information transfer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  "The requirements of this section shall be equally applicable to all subcontractors of a terminated contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(a)(3) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, application to subcontractors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1061(a)) rather than independently authored sources. The retention obligation itself — what the successor contractor must then do with that employee information — is addressed in a separate clause of this document, sourced to § 1061(b).

THE 60-DAY RETENTION OBLIGATION AND ITS CAUSE EXCEPTION
The core obligation the Act imposes is a retention requirement, not a general job-security guarantee: a successor contractor or successor subcontractor must retain, for a 60-day transition employment period, each employee who was employed by the terminated contractor or its subcontractors for the preceding four months or longer at the site(s) now covered by the successor service contract. The one statutory exception is narrow — the successor need not hire a particular employee if it has "reasonable and substantiated cause," and that cause must be based on the employee's own performance or conduct while working under the terminated contract, not on cost, headcount reduction as such, or any other unrelated ground. The statute also requires that this retention requirement be disclosed in advance: awarding authorities must state it in all initial bid packages governed by the chapter, so that anyone bidding on a covered contract knows the retention obligation will apply if awarded.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "A successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall retain, for a 60-day transition employment period, employees who have been employed by the terminated contractor or its subcontractors, if any, for the preceding four months or longer at the site or sites covered by the successor service contract unless the successor contractor or successor subcontractor has reasonable and substantiated cause not to hire a particular employee based on that employee’s performance or conduct while working under the terminated contract. This requirement shall be stated by awarding authorities in all initial bid packages that are governed by this chapter."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(b)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, 60-day retention requirement and cause exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: The quote below is a single subdivision (Labor Code § 1061(b)(1)) of the statutory section covering retention. Note for anyone researching a physical notice-posting requirement: this section does not impose one. The disclosure mechanism the statute actually specifies is inclusion of the retention requirement in awarding authorities' initial bid packages — not a workplace posting. No posting requirement appears anywhere in Labor Code §§ 1060-1065 as verified for this document; if a posting requirement exists for building-service transitions, it would have to come from a source outside this chapter (for example, a local ordinance under § 1064, discussed in a separate clause of this document), which was not researched here.

WRITTEN OFFER TERMS AND SENIORITY WHEN FEWER EMPLOYEES ARE NEEDED
Where the retention obligation applies, the Act specifies how the offer itself must be made, not just that it must be made. The successor contractor or successor subcontractor must give each covered employee a written offer of employment in that employee's primary language, or another language the employee is literate in, and the offer must state a deadline to accept that is no shorter than 10 days. Notably, the statute does not require wage or benefit matching: nothing in the chapter obligates the successor to pay the same wages or offer the same benefits the terminated contractor or subcontractor provided. If the successor determines it needs fewer employees than the terminated contractor used at the same site(s), it cannot pick and choose freely among the otherwise-eligible employees — it must retain by seniority within each job classification.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall make a written offer of employment to each employee, as required by this section, in the employee’s primary language or another language in which the employee is literate. That offer shall state the time within which the employee must accept that offer, but in no case may that time be less than 10 days. Nothing in this section requires the successor contractor or successor subcontractor to pay the same wages or offer the same benefits as were provided by the prior contractor or prior subcontractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(b)(2) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, written offer requirements (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  "If at any time the successor contractor or successor subcontractor determines that fewer employees are needed to perform services under the successor service contract or successor subcontract than were required by the terminated contractor under the terminated contract or terminated subcontract, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall retain employees by seniority within the job classification."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(b)(3) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, seniority-based retention when fewer employees are needed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1061(b)(2)-(3)) as the retention obligation covered in a separate clause of this document.

EMPLOYEE LISTS AND THE PREFERENTIAL HIRING LIST
The Act builds in reporting obligations meant to make retention decisions checkable. Once the successor contractor or successor subcontractor begins service under the successor contract, it must give the awarding authority a list of its own employees and its subcontractors' employees working at the covered site(s), indicating which of them were previously employed there by the terminated contractor or subcontractor. It must also provide a separate list identifying any of the terminated contractor's employees who were not retained, together with the stated reason each was not retained. During the 60-day transition period itself, the successor must maintain a preferential hiring list of eligible covered employees it did not initially retain, and must hire additional employees from that list until every one of the terminated contractor's or subcontractor's employees has been offered employment with the successor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall also provide a list of any of the terminated contractor’s employees who were not retained either by the successor contractor or successor subcontractor, stating the reason these employees were not retained."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, employee-list disclosure to the awarding authority (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  "During the 60-day transition employment period, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall maintain a preferential hiring list of eligible covered employees not retained by the successor contractor or successor subcontractor from which the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall hire additional employees until such time as all of the terminated contractor’s or terminated subcontractor’s employees have been offered employment with the successor contractor or successor subcontractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(d) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, preferential hiring list during the transition period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: The two quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1061(c)-(d)).

PROTECTION AGAINST DISCHARGE WITHOUT CAUSE, AND WHAT HAPPENS AFTER 60 DAYS
Retention under the Act carries a corresponding job-security floor during the transition period itself: for the initial 60-day transition employment period, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor may not discharge a retained employee without cause, and cause has to rest only on that particular employee's own performance or conduct. At the end of the 60-day period, the statute requires a written performance evaluation for each retained employee. If that employee's performance during the 60 days was satisfactory, the successor must offer continued employment. The Act's protections are time-limited, however: employment after the 60-day transition period converts to ordinary at-will employment, under which the employee may then be terminated without cause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "During the initial 60-day transition employment period, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall not discharge without cause an employee retained pursuant to this chapter. Cause shall be based only on the performance or conduct of the particular employee."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(e) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, no discharge without cause during the transition period (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  "At the end of the 60-day transition employment period, a successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall provide a written performance evaluation to each employee retained pursuant to this chapter. If the employee’s performance during that 60-day period is satisfactory, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall offer the employee continued employment. Any employment after the 60-day transition employment period shall be at-will employment under which the employee may be terminated without cause."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1061(f) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, end-of-period evaluation and transition to at-will employment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1061.)
  Known gap: The two quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1061(e)-(f)).

EFFECTIVE DATE AND WHAT THE ACT DOES NOT CHANGE
The Act's obligations are not open-ended in time or in reach. By its own terms, the chapter applies only to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2002. And apart from the notice and retention obligations specifically described in Labor Code § 1061(a) and (b), the chapter does not otherwise change or expand the legal relationship or duties between a property owner or awarding authority (or their agents) and contractors, subcontractors, or their employees. The Act also does not restrict a property owner's or awarding authority's underlying business decisions: nothing in the chapter limits the right to terminate a service contract, to replace one contractor with another, or to bring building maintenance in-house using the property owner's or awarding authority's own employees — the retention obligation applies to whichever party ends up as the successor employer of the covered work, not to the decision of whether to make that change at all.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "This chapter only applies to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2002."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1063(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, effective date of coverage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1063.)
  "Except for the obligations specified in subdivisions (a) and (b) of Section 1061, nothing in this chapter changes or increases the relationship or duties of a property owner or an awarding authority, or their agents, with respect to contractors, subcontractors, or their employees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1063(b) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, no expansion of duties beyond the notice and retention obligations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1063.)
  "Nothing in this chapter limits the right of a property owner or an awarding authority to terminate a service contract or to replace a contractor with another contractor or with the property owner’s or awarding authority’s own employees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1063(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, no limit on the right to terminate or replace a contractor (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1063.)
  Known gap: All three quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1063). This document does not separately research or verify whether any particular local government ordinance imposes greater standards than this chapter, though § 1064 (not quoted in this document) expressly permits local agencies to enact such ordinances.

HOW THE ACT IS ENFORCED
The Act is enforced through a private right of action, not a state agency complaint process. An employee who was not offered employment in violation of the chapter, or who was discharged in violation of it, or an agent of that employee, may sue the successor contractor or successor subcontractor in California superior court. On a finding of violation, the court must award backpay (including the value of benefits) for each day the violation has occurred and continues, calculated as whichever is greater of two measures: the employee's average regular rate of pay over the last three years in the same occupational classification, multiplied by average hours worked over that same three-year period, or the employee's final regular rate of pay at the time the predecessor contract terminated, multiplied by the employee's usual hours. Courts may also order a preliminary or permanent injunction against continued violation, and a prevailing employee is entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs. One limit built into the enforcement scheme: absent an underlying claim that the employee was terminated in violation of the chapter, an employee cannot sue solely because the employer failed to provide the end-of-period written performance evaluation described elsewhere in this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "An employee, who was not offered employment or who has been discharged in violation of this chapter by a successor contractor or successor subcontractor, or an agent of the employee may bring an action against a successor contractor or successor subcontractor in any superior court of the State of California having jurisdiction over the successor contractor or successor subcontractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1062(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, private right of action and mandatory backpay (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1062.)
  "Upon finding a violation of this chapter, the court shall award backpay, including the value of benefits, for each day during which the violation has occurred and continues to occur."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1062(a) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, backpay measure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1062.)
  "The court may order a preliminary or permanent injunction to stop the continued violation of this chapter."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1062(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, injunctive relief and attorney's fees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1062.)
  "In the absence of a claim by an employee that he or she was terminated in violation of this chapter, an employee may not maintain a cause of action under this chapter solely for the failure of an employer to provide a written performance evaluation."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1062(d) (California Legislative Information, official text), California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, limit on evaluation-only claims (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1062.)

citations.quote: During the 60-day transition employment period, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall maintain a preferential hiring list of eligible covered employees not retained by the successor contractor or successor subcontractor from which the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall hire additional employees until such time as all of the terminated contractor’s or terminated subcontractor’s employees have been offered employment with the successor contractor or successor subcontractor.

expectedJSON.body: Retention under the Act carries a corresponding job-security floor during the transition period itself: for the initial 60-day transition employment period, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor may not discharge a retained employee without cause, and cause has to rest only on that particular employee's own performance or conduct. At the end of the 60-day period, the statute requires a written performance evaluation for each retained employee. If that employee's performance during the 60 days was satisfactory, the successor must offer continued employment. The Act's protections are time-limited, however: employment after the 60-day transition period converts to ordinary at-will employment, under which the employee may then be terminated without cause.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1061(e) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, no discharge without cause during the transition period
citations.quote: During the initial 60-day transition employment period, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall not discharge without cause an employee retained pursuant to this chapter. Cause shall be based only on the performance or conduct of the particular employee.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1061(f) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, end-of-period evaluation and transition to at-will employment
citations.quote: At the end of the 60-day transition employment period, a successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall provide a written performance evaluation to each employee retained pursuant to this chapter. If the employee’s performance during that 60-day period is satisfactory, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall offer the employee continued employment. Any employment after the 60-day transition employment period shall be at-will employment under which the employee may be terminated without cause.

expectedJSON.body: The Act's obligations are not open-ended in time or in reach. By its own terms, the chapter applies only to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2002. And apart from the notice and retention obligations specifically described in Labor Code § 1061(a) and (b), the chapter does not otherwise change or expand the legal relationship or duties between a property owner or awarding authority (or their agents) and contractors, subcontractors, or their employees. The Act also does not restrict a property owner's or awarding authority's underlying business decisions: nothing in the chapter limits the right to terminate a service contract, to replace one contractor with another, or to bring building maintenance in-house using the property owner's or awarding authority's own employees — the retention obligation applies to whichever party ends up as the successor employer of the covered work, not to the decision of whether to make that change at all.

expectedJSON.body: The Act is enforced through a private right of action, not a state agency complaint process. An employee who was not offered employment in violation of the chapter, or who was discharged in violation of it, or an agent of that employee, may sue the successor contractor or successor subcontractor in California superior court. On a finding of violation, the court must award backpay (including the value of benefits) for each day the violation has occurred and continues, calculated as whichever is greater of two measures: the employee's average regular rate of pay over the last three years in the same occupational classification, multiplied by average hours worked over that same three-year period, or the employee's final regular rate of pay at the time the predecessor contract terminated, multiplied by the employee's usual hours. Courts may also order a preliminary or permanent injunction against continued violation, and a prevailing employee is entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs. One limit built into the enforcement scheme: absent an underlying claim that the employee was terminated in violation of the chapter, an employee cannot sue solely because the employer failed to provide the end-of-period written performance evaluation described elsewhere in this document.

citations.quote: An employee, who was not offered employment or who has been discharged in violation of this chapter by a successor contractor or successor subcontractor, or an agent of the employee may bring an action against a successor contractor or successor subcontractor in any superior court of the State of California having jurisdiction over the successor contractor or successor subcontractor.
